title: Could Saturn really float in water?

hook.banner: Could Saturn really float in water?

narration.heading: Saturn
narration.text: You've heard Saturn could float in a bathtub. Let's find out if that's true.

narration.heading: Giant
narration.text: Saturn is about nine times wider than Earth. Some seven hundred and sixty Earths could fit inside.

narration.heading: Fast spin
narration.text: Yet it spins so fast, a day here lasts only about ten and a half hours.

narration.heading: The rings
narration.text: Its rings reach out two hundred and eighty-two thousand kilometres from the planet.

narration.heading: Paper thin
narration.text: But the main rings are typically only about ten metres thick.

narration.heading: The hexagon
narration.text: At the north pole spins a giant hexagon. Each side is longer than Earth is wide.

narration.heading: The winds
narration.text: Winds here can blow at one thousand eight hundred kilometres an hour.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? Saturn's average density is lower than water's. It's the only planet like that.

narration.heading: The bathtub
narration.text: So find a bathtub big enough, and NASA says it could float. What would you drop in next?

skit.text: Saturn floats? Great. I sink. I've tested it. Once.

titles: What if you dropped Saturn in a giant bathtub?
Saturn is less dense than water
youtube.description: A spin around Saturn: its paper-thin rings, the hexagon storm at its north pole and 1,800 km/h winds, and why NASA says it could float in a big enough bathtub.

sources.claim: Saturn is about 9 times wider than Earth; its rings reach up to 282,000 km from the planet and the main rings are typically about 10 m thick; it is the only planet less dense than water and could float in a big enough bathtub
Saturn's mean radius is 58,232 km; volume 763.59 Earths; mean density 0.6871 g/cm³, the only planet less dense than water; a day lasts about 10.5 hours; axial tilt 26.73°
Saturn's north polar hexagon is centred near 78° N, each side about 14,500 km, longer than Earth's diameter; winds reach up to 1,800 km/h
